title: Fed Holds Rates but Suffers Its Most Fractured Hawkish Dissent in Decades, and Bond Markets Now Bet on a September Hike
summary: The Federal Reserve left its policy rate unchanged at its July meeting, but three regional presidents dissented in favour of an immediate hike and Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish tone left bond markets pricing a much higher chance of a September rise. The vote matters less for the rate itself than for what it shows about a Fed under new leadership that has stripped out forward guidance, making each meeting a fresh, harder-to-predict event rather than a step along a signalled path.
context:
- Warsh took over as chair earlier in 2026 and dropped the explicit forward guidance that previous FOMC statements relied on, shifting the Fed to a meeting-by-meeting stance that leaves investors reacting to each data print and speech rather than following a telegraphed plan.

- The three dissents, from Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Minneapolis's Neel Kashkari and Dallas's Lorie Logan, were unified around wanting a hike rather than split between easing and tightening camps — the first time since September 2016 that dissenters have aligned on a single direction, and read by some analysts as the most fractured hawkish vote since the 1970s.

- Warsh has repeatedly described inflation as "a choice" in public remarks, framing a tougher policy stance as central to rebuilding the Fed's credibility after criticism of the prior leadership's handling of the post-pandemic inflation spike.

- Futures markets moved to price a substantially higher probability of a September hike within the same session as the announcement, illustrating how far Warsh's rhetoric outran what his own committee actually voted to do this time.

- Longer-dated Treasury yields pushing to their highest levels in nearly two decades reflects markets repricing not just the near-term rate path but the long-run inflation and fiscal risk premium under a Fed leadership seen as less tolerant of above-target inflation.

title: Big Tech's AI Spending Splits Into Winners and Losers: Microsoft and Amazon Rewarded, Meta and Alphabet Punished
summary: This week's second-quarter results from Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Alphabet and Apple showed investors starting to discriminate sharply between companies whose AI capital spending shows up as measurable revenue and those where it remains a matter of faith. The split matters because it marks a break from two years in which nearly any AI capex announcement was rewarded uniformly, regardless of whether a clear monetisation path existed.
context:
- Combined AI capital expenditure across Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft is on track to reach roughly $725 billion in 2026, up around 77% on 2025 — a scale of spending large enough that investors are now demanding evidence of a direct return rather than treating capex as a proxy for future growth.

- Microsoft and Amazon were rewarded because their AI investment feeds directly into metered, externally billed cloud revenue through Azure and AWS, giving investors a legible, quantifiable link between spending and income.

- Meta and Alphabet's declines reflect investor unease that consumer-facing and advertising-driven AI investment is harder to trace to incremental revenue, even though both companies, like their peers, posted double-digit overall revenue growth.

- Apple's fall points to a different worry: perceived lag in proprietary AI capability relative to its large-cap peers, despite Apple not carrying anything like the same scale of infrastructure capex.

- The divergence signals a shift away from the "rising tide lifts all AI boats" dynamic of the past two years toward a more selective market that is starting to separate AI spending with a visible revenue path from spending still justified mainly by future promise.

title: US Growth Slows to 1.5% While Price Pressures Accelerate, Reviving the Stagflation Debate
summary: The advance estimate of second-quarter US GDP showed growth decelerating to a 1.5% annualised pace even as the price index for gross domestic purchases accelerated sharply, reviving talk of a stagflation-like mix of weaker growth and stronger inflation. The report matters because it complicates the binary framing of the Fed's dilemma, suggesting policymakers may face slowing activity and rising price pressure at the same time rather than being able to trade one off against the other.
context:
- The 1.5% growth rate was a marked deceleration from 2.1% in the first quarter and came in below economists' expectations, with the drag driven partly by imports rising faster than exports rather than by a broad-based slowdown in domestic demand.

- Consumer spending, which accounts for roughly 70% of US economic activity, actually accelerated to a 3.2% pace from a soft 0.5% at the start of the year, indicating the growth slowdown was not primarily a story of retrenching households.

- Business investment excluding housing grew at an 8.4% annualised rate, moderating from 10.6% in the first quarter but still historically elevated, with the report specifically pointing to continued heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure as a key driver.

- The price index for gross domestic purchases rose 5.7%, a sharp acceleration from 3.6% in the prior quarter, arriving just a day after the Fed held rates while explicitly flagging inflation as its dominant concern.

- The combination of slowing headline growth alongside accelerating price pressures is the classic pairing markets read as a stagflation warning, reinforcing the view forming this week that the Fed may be confronting both risks rising together rather than a simple choice between supporting growth and containing inflation.
